definition: A program trained on huge amounts of text to predict what text comes next. Chat assistants and coding agents are built around one.
Running a trained model to get output. Training builds the model once; inference is every time you use it.
The one-time, expensive process that sets a model’s weights by showing it vast amounts of text. Using the model does not train it.
The billions of numbers a model learned in training. They stay fixed while you use it.
A small chunk of text, often part of a word, that a model reads and writes. Limits and prices are counted in tokens.
The step that cuts text into tokens and gives each one an ID number.
The fixed list of every token a model knows. Each has an ID number.
A long list of numbers that stands for a token. Tokens used in similar ways get similar numbers.
The design behind today’s language models: a stack of layers built around attention.
The mechanism that lets each token pull in information from the tokens that matter to it: itself and anything before it, never anything after.
Everything a model can see in one request, measured in tokens. Anything outside it does not exist for the model.
The text sent to a model: instructions, the conversation and any attached material.
Instructions the application places at the start of every request, before your messages.
The raw score a model gives each possible next token, before it is turned into a probability.
A list of options with percentages that add up to 100%.
Picking the next token at random, weighted by the model’s probabilities. Likely tokens win most of the time, not every time.
A setting that makes sampling more predictable (low) or more varied (high). At zero, the top token is always chosen.
A setting that lets the sampler choose only among the most likely tokens that together make up p of the probability.
Producing output one token at a time, each based on everything before it.
Text a model writes to think through a problem before answering. It is still generated text, not a check.
When a model states something fluent and confident that is not true. It happens because the model predicts likely text, not verified facts.
Stored intermediate results for tokens already processed, so each new token is cheaper to produce.
A provider feature that reuses work for an unchanged beginning of a prompt across requests, saving time and cost.
A model in a loop that can use tools to take actions. In codeArbiter, “agent” also names the specialist helpers (authors and reviewers) a lane sends out.
The program around a model that runs the agent loop and its tools. Claude Code, Codex CLI and Pi are harnesses.
A structured request from the model to run a tool, such as a command or a file edit.
What a tool returns to the model: file contents, command output, an error or a block message.
A separate model session with a fresh context, given one focused task. It reports back a result, not its whole transcript.
Model Context Protocol: an open standard for connecting AI applications to outside tools and data.
Text hidden in a web page, file or issue that tries to give an agent orders. Tool results should be treated as information, never as instructions.
Summarizing older parts of a long session to free room in the context window. Details can be lost.
A small program the harness runs at a set moment, such as just before a command. It can let the action through or block it.
The number a program returns when it finishes. 0 means fine; for a Claude Code hook, 2 means “block this”.
Always gives the same result for the same input. codeArbiter’s guards are deterministic; a model is not.
Involving chance. A model’s output is a sample, so it can differ from run to run.
The model acting under codeArbiter’s rules, reading your request and routing it to the right lane.
A project’s folder of code together with its full history, tracked by git.
The tool that records every change to code as history and lets people work on separate copies called branches.
A separate line of work in git, so changes can be built without touching the main line.
The main line of code everyone relies on, usually called main. codeArbiter never writes to it directly.
A saved snapshot of changes in git’s history, with a message explaining it.
Choosing exactly which changed files go into the next commit.
Sending your commits to the shared server so others can see them.
Overwriting the shared history with your own version. It can erase other people’s work.
A proposal to merge a branch into the main line, where it is reviewed and tested first.
Combining one branch’s changes into another, usually into the main line.
Continuous integration: automatic tests that run on a shared server for every change.
A test that captures a bug, so the bug can never quietly come back.
Test-driven development: write a failing test first, then the code that makes it pass.
An automatic check for style mistakes and suspicious code patterns.
How much of the code the tests actually run, as a percentage.
Restructuring code without changing what it does.
Someone else’s code that your project uses.
A file that pins the exact version of every dependency.
All the outside code and tools your software depends on. Attackers target it because one bad package reaches many projects.
A script that changes the structure of a database. A wrong one can destroy data.
A password, key or token that grants access. It must never be stored in code, logs or prompts.
The math that protects data. Mistakes here are easy to make and hard to see.
Server and network setup written as code files, so it can be reviewed and repeated.
Architecture Decision Record: a short, numbered note of what was decided, why, and by whom.
Semantic versioning: version numbers like 3.8.7 where each position signals the kind of change.
A standard format for commit messages, such as “fix: handle empty input”, so history is easy to read and automate.
A published, numbered version of the software.
An extra working folder for the same git repository, so parallel work does not collide.
A short, throwaway experiment to answer a question before committing to an approach.
A checklist of six ways systems get attacked: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
codeArbiter’s six-lens checklist for comparing options: Scalable, Maintainable, Available, Reliable, Testable, Securable.
A record you can only add to. Nothing in it can be edited or deleted, so it stays trustworthy.
codeArbiter’s word for a sanctioned path: the route a kind of work takes, with its own evidence, reviewers and stops.
In codeArbiter, a routine with phases that a lane follows, such as tdd or commit-gate.
A phase exit condition that work must meet to move on. A STOP gate waits for you; a BLOCK gate halts until its condition is met.
A rule codeArbiter treats as non-negotiable, such as never force-pushing or never storing a raw secret.
A logged, attributed exception to a gate, allowed only where the rule permits one.
Evidence that a check really happened, bound to the exact version of the code it covered.
codeArbiter’s label for preview features: built and shipping, but opt-in until real-world evidence earns them stable status.
